blocks.text: Why I want to keep this question within theology
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: Much of the argument applies across higher education. That was one reason I kept asking how to make it a substantive question in theological pedagogy rather than simply placing a general assessment problem in a theology faculty. I had considered theology broadly and wondered whether a narrower field would help. Science and Religion became a possible setting because it could specify the kind of understanding at stake. The example about methodological and metaphysical naturalism suggests one manageable problem: recognising which claims a scientific explanation supports, where additional philosophical commitments enter, and how a theological argument uses or challenges those commitments. This remains a possible focus, rather than a research design already chosen or validated.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: An earlier discussion of adapting my existing framework had exposed a related distinction. The assistant warned that replacing computing components with theological ones might offer limited novelty, particularly given an existing biology adaptation. I objected that adequacy in theology had not been demonstrated by success in another field. Novelty and validity were separate questions. The objection did not prove that a straightforward adaptation would make a strong dissertation; it clarified why disciplinary transfer could itself require substantive examination. I wanted to know whether the framework's assumptions about evidence, judgment and responsibility remained defensible in theology, and which of those assumptions mattered most urgently for teaching and assessment.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: In such a setting, grammatical fluency and successful paraphrase would provide incomplete evidence. I would want to know whether the student can identify the premises, explain why the distinction matters and assess an objection from another position. The relevant standards would need to come from the actual theological and philosophical inquiry. They could not be obtained simply by relabelling a general measure of textual similarity as a measure of theological understanding.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: Theology also makes the relationship between receiving and judging especially visible to me. Studying it involves sustained engagement with texts, traditions, teachers and arguments whose claims I did not originate. My contribution can include learning to interpret those claims responsibly and to understand the grounds on which they should be accepted, qualified or rejected. Recognising that dependence does not make all sources equivalent. It makes the justification of their authority, and my responsibility in responding to them, part of the educational task.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: Recent theological scholarship confirms that this is already an active conversation. Wang argues for integrating AI literacy, institutional policy and classroom experimentation in theological education, developing a proposal for partnership between human learners and AI (Wang, 2026). I take that as a relevant position to engage, rather than evidence that the learning question has been settled. My narrower concern is what would warrant a judgment that such a partnership has developed theological understanding. Learning to elicit a persuasive theological answer and learning to assess the answer's premises, sources and implications may overlap, but the relationship needs to be demonstrated.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: Wang's article combines a proposal for theological education with reports of practice, including a survey receiving 34 responses from faculty and staff across fifteen Hong Kong seminaries. It also describes his development of a sermon-preparation GPT and possible classroom uses, including simulated conversations with theological figures (Wang, 2026, pp. 65–67). These details provide concrete practices to examine, while stopping short of a controlled demonstration of improved theological understanding. That distinction lets me take the proposal seriously without turning reported enthusiasm, institutional activity or the author's account of learning through tool design into evidence for every educational claim.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: The simulated interlocutor raises a specifically interpretive problem. A model speaking in a theologian's voice may help me formulate a question, yet its reply is not historical evidence that the theologian held that position. I would need to compare it with relevant texts and distinguish quotation, reconstruction and imaginative extension. The same concern applies when a tutor presents a synthesis across traditions: which disagreements has it preserved, and which has it smoothed away? These are questions for investigation, rather than findings about every system. They identify where technical design and theological judgment meet—through source selection, instructions, generated explanations and the student's ability to recognise the status of what is being offered.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: For example, the distinction between methodological and metaphysical naturalism could be recited accurately while being applied badly. A learner might explain that a scientific method restricts certain kinds of explanation, then mistakenly treat that methodological restriction as a proof about everything that exists. Conversely, a learner could challenge an argument's metaphysical step without rejecting the scientific finding on which it draws. These are proposed contrasts for examining understanding, not observations from a completed study. They show why the disciplinary content matters: a generic measure of semantic resemblance could miss the precise inference whose legitimacy is in dispute.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: I would also need to state which educational purpose is at issue. An academic study of theological arguments, preparation for ministry and formation within a particular faith community need not assess identical achievements. My immediate question concerns the student's interpretive and argumentative judgment; it does not presume that agreement with a theological conclusion demonstrates understanding, or that an assessor can infer a person's faith from polished prose. A useful framework should make such differences explicit rather than allowing “theological formation” to become a name for several unexamined outcomes.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: This keeps the technical inquiry relevant. Understanding how models acquire and use representations could help explain what kinds of distinctions their responses preserve, reconstruct or obscure. HCI could examine how a learner engages with those responses. Value Sensitive Design could help investigate how assessment arrangements distribute responsibility and how they balance transparency, fairness and educational opportunity. None of these perspectives can establish the whole case alone, and a model's internal behaviour would remain different evidence from a student's learning.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: Value Sensitive Design offers a way to keep those inquiries connected. Friedman, Kahn and Borning describe an approach combining conceptual, empirical and technical investigation (Friedman, Kahn and Borning, 2008). Applied to this problem, the conceptual work asks what understanding and responsible contribution mean; the empirical work examines how students and teachers actually interpret and use assistance; the technical work examines what a system enables, records or obscures. These investigations should constrain one another. A demand for complete interaction logs might improve visibility while creating burdens of privacy, access and interpretation. Those tensions belong inside the design of assessment evidence, rather than being treated as administrative details after a technical system has been built.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: The supplied VSD text made me reconsider how confidently I could import the framework. It is a 2013 reprint of a 2006 chapter, with an addendum by Alina Huldtgren, rather than simply the 2008 handbook version cited earlier. The addendum discusses criticism of predetermined value lists and distinguishes values explicitly supported by a system, values held by stakeholders and values held by designers (Huldtgren, 2013, pp. 85–88). This is directly relevant to adaptation in theology. Agreement that “understanding,” “fairness” or “formation” matters does not establish agreement about what each requires. My existing framework supplies resources for inquiry; its categories must also remain open to challenge from the people and practices it is intended to serve.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: A case in the original chapter makes the iterative method tangible. While redesigning browser consent, the researchers found that excessive interruption could undermine informed consent itself, leading them to add minimal distraction to their account of the value being supported (Friedman, Kahn and Borning, 2006/2013, pp. 62–63). My analogous concern is a demand for exhaustive AI disclosure: documentation intended to support responsible judgment might become burdensome ritual. That is a design hypothesis, not an established effect in theological assessment. It would need investigation with students and teachers, including those indirectly affected by how records are interpreted.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: This also suggests a more fundamental role for programming than measuring how many words AI changed. A research system could make competing assumptions about contribution and evidence explicit, then examine how different policy rules classify the same documented sequence of suggestion, criticism, revision and later explanation. Visualisation could reveal where a judgment depends on information the record does not contain. This is a possible extension emerging from the review, rather than a validated method for inferring authorship from a transcript. Its value would depend on whether it exposes consequential assumptions that ordinary discussion leaves hidden, while allowing the theological judgments themselves to remain contestable.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: Kane's caution that validation is systematic without being automatic helps define the computational boundary (Kane, 2013, p. 64). A program could expose which conclusions follow only after a disputed assumption is added, or show how the same record receives different interpretations under different assessment purposes. It could not establish that the assumption is educationally justified merely by executing it consistently. For an MSt, a manageable contribution might be a tightly bounded analysis of one such inference in Science and Religion, with a small computational demonstration if it genuinely assists that analysis. A possible DPhil could investigate the resulting claims empirically across interactions and assessment settings. Those are possible scales of inquiry, not a settled project or a promise of validated automation.
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: For me, this extends the question behind my previous assessment work. A framework can make permissions, disclosure and evidence more explicit. It still depends on assumptions about what the evidence establishes. The next inquiry may need to examine those assumptions themselves: when does an interaction support the learner's intellectual development, when does it substitute for a capacity being assessed, and how should uncertainty affect an institutional judgment?
blocks.section: Why I want to keep this question within theology

blocks.text: The conversation belongs inside the problem
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: The exchange through which I reached these questions is itself relevant evidence of a process, although it cannot validate that process simply by describing it favourably. I brought the concern about the policy, the comparison with friends and professors, and the example of returning to AI-assisted writing as a learner. The AI articulated distinctions, retrieved documents and offered possible research directions. I rejected several formulations because they narrowed the technical question too quickly or answered a different case from the one I had posed. Those interventions were intellectual actions even when they consisted of a short question or a request to reconsider an answer. The archive records more polished formulations supplied by AI alongside the objections that made those formulations change. Counting the words each participant produced would miss part of that causal history.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: The assistant's hypothetical example about naturalism helped give the final difficulty a concrete form. Its repeated qualifications also became part of what I had to examine. I could agree that understanding differs from origination, or that feedback differs from someone writing a complete proposal, while still finding that those correct statements did not answer the comparison. Some progress consisted in identifying why an apparently careful reply was insufficient.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: There is a further caution in reconstructing the dialogue. My persistence does not prove that my criticism was correct, and the model's eventual agreement is not independent confirmation. The visible exchange shows that its replies changed after my objections; it does not establish the internal mechanism responsible for that change. I cannot infer a particular training objective or an institutional motive from the transcript. The criticism has to be assessed through the comparison, the documentary evidence and the reasons offered, including the possibility that a relevant difference between cases has been overlooked.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: Technical research supplies a reason to take that caution seriously without diagnosing this particular exchange. Sharma and colleagues found sycophantic behaviour in the assistants they studied and evidence that optimisation against human preference models can favour agreement with a user's views over truthfulness (Sharma et al., 2024). This creates a question about educational alignment: an interaction that satisfies my immediate preference for reassurance may fail to help me recognise a weak argument. Yet disagreement would not automatically be evidence of better tutoring either. The relevant aim would be responsiveness to reasons, including the possibility that my objection is sound. Establishing that responsiveness requires evidence beyond the model's agreeable tone or my satisfaction with its answer.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: The study's methods also discourage a simplified story about alignment inevitably producing agreement. Sharma and colleagues separately varied users' stated preferences, examined changes to answers after challenge, and investigated optimisation against preference models. The effects of optimisation differed across methods and measures; some forms of sycophancy were already present before reinforcement learning (Sharma et al., 2024, pp. 3, 7–9). The pedagogical issue therefore becomes more specific: which design choices favour reassurance, correction or reasoned reconsideration, and under what conditions? In theology, where legitimate disagreement may concern premises as well as conclusions, responsiveness cannot mean enforcing one answer indiscriminately. A useful tutor would need to help expose the disagreement and its grounds without treating my preference as evidence that my position is sound.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: Reconstructing the exchange now adds another layer. The conversation record helps me distinguish what I initially asked from what became articulable later. It also leaves room for a polished account to make the development look more coherent than it felt while it was happening. I do not want to erase the repetitions or imply that I had already formulated the eventual criticism at the beginning. AI participated in the formulation of that criticism, including its expression here. That participation is part of the authorship question the article examines.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: The point at which the AI agreed that the policy was weak was also the point at which I asked to leave the question open. That decision matters to the history of the inquiry. Agreement had given the concern a clearer formulation, but it had not produced a rule that classified every case. Saying that an applicant must retain substantive intellectual judgment points toward something important, while leaving further questions about what counts as substantive, how development should be demonstrated and what burdens of documentation are reasonable. The same is true of treating comparable human and AI assistance comparably: the relevant similarities and differences must still be investigated in particular educational settings.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: The further literature has made that openness more demanding. It challenges an ideal of thinking without intellectual dependence, provides evidence that assistance can either support or undermine the acquisition of skills, and documents institutional uncertainty. It also gives me reasons to distrust an easy defence of my own practice: felt ownership, fluent explanation and a preserved dialogue each provide incomplete evidence. The intellectual task is to connect those kinds of evidence to a specific educational claim without allowing one to stand in for all the others.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: Closer reading also changes how I would state a positive finding about my own practice. A claim that I learned from an AI-assisted text, a claim that I can now exercise a capacity independently, and a claim that I deserve credit for originating its argument require different histories and evidence. They can become warranted at different times. Later understanding does not erase earlier assistance; earlier assistance does not settle what I can subsequently learn. This temporal distinction is perhaps the most useful development of the original threefold account. It allows the work to remain a record of contribution while also becoming material through which its maker changes.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: What changed was the question I wanted to pursue. Initially, I hoped a clearer technical account of AI might help explain whether certain uses should be allowed. I now also want to know whether the categories used to permit and prohibit those uses adequately describe the learning they regulate. Feedback can help bring an idea into existence. An externally suggested idea can become something a learner understands, develops and takes responsibility for. The extent of that development cannot be settled by its origin alone.
blocks.section: The conversation belongs inside the problem

blocks.text: I want to leave the comparison open at precisely that point. If I critically develop the same suggestion through the same intellectual work, what educationally relevant difference would justify accepting the assistance from a friend and rejecting it from AI? If there is such a difference, how should we establish it? If there is not, what would an adequate policy have to recognise?
